source.title: The Slow Deterioration of the Generalization Error of the Random Feature Model
source.authors: Chao Ma; Lei Wu; E. Weinan

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures test error across random-feature model sizes and along gradient-descent trajectories. This is a different model class and experimental setting from deep networks, but it directly tests broader double-descent and training-time behavior.
record.gate_note: Reported test-error curves and explicit descriptions of those curves are included. Eigenvalue spectra are not rows because they do not measure a claim version's test-error behavior. Results cited from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study measures test error of random-feature models across feature counts and along gradient-descent time. It shows the min-norm curve peaks at m=n. It argues the peak is 'washed out by the dynamics' at practical training lengths, which is a specific restatement of the model-wise curve and bears on the epoch-wise and regularization versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is correct. It should add the authors' framing that the double-descent peak is 'washed out by the dynamics' at practical training lengths. They also say the overfitting comes from GD fitting small-eigenvalue directions, not from over-parametrization.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes random feature regression and GD/gradient-flow trajectories rather than reproducing the original deep-network experiments. It compares minimum-norm and finite-time solutions and develops a theoretical account of slow deterioration.
record.method_sensitivity: The observed test-error behavior varies with feature count relative to sample size, training time, and feature choice (ReLU versus indicator features).

fits_no_version.finding: The time to reach the eventual test error grows with its size, and test-error growth after the initial descent is bounded by c√t, both theoretically (Theorem 1, Corollary 2) and empirically.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Near the interpolation threshold, overfitting along GD develops slowly (∝√t), giving a long early-stopping window.

record.peer_reviewed: Mathematical and Scientific Machine Learning, Proceedings of Machine Learning Research, vol. 107 (2020)
record.problems: Experimental curve values are mostly presented in figures rather than stated numerically. The experiments concern random feature models, not deep networks; the authors leave study of two-layer neural networks for future work.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix Figures 6–7 report Gram-matrix spectra and smallest-eigenvalue behavior, not test-error outcomes named by the claim versions, so they are not rows.

untested.parts: All of V1: no deep networks are studied; only random feature models.
All of V3: there is no sample-size sweep.
Model classes other than random-feature regression.
All of V5: no single effective-complexity measure is tested across axes.
Label-noise dependence, multiple peaks, and optimally tuned explicit regularization.
All of V7: there is no re-counting of effective parameters.

missing.what: MNIST test error along the GD path at m=n=500: it stays small over a long interval, then increases to a large value. This is an epoch-wise fall-plateau-rise result on real data.

record.verdict_notes: r8 duplicates r3. Rows r4–r7 were mis-linked to V2 with wrong conditions (d=10, m=n=500), though they come from the MNIST model-wise sweep in Fig 1(c). Evidence is mostly qualitative figure descriptions. The V6 label rests on reading finite-time GD as implicit regularization; the paper does not tune explicit regularization.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses random feature models, not deep networks, so it does not test model-wise double descent in deep networks.
The tested trajectories use gradient-descent time, not a sweep over training epochs in deep networks; the paper does not report a fall-rise-fall trajectory.
No sweep over training sample size near an interpolation threshold is reported.
The study tests random feature models, not multiple model classes. Its model-size curves compare minimum-norm solutions with finite-time GD solutions.
The study does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, time, and sample-size axes.
The study does not test label-noise dependence, multiple peaks, or optimally tuned regularization.
The study does not re-count complexity using an effective number of parameters or test whether that makes the curve U-shaped.

rows.subject: random feature models
rows.size_stated: m/n=0.9 and 1.1; also m/n=1/2 and 2; other plotted values include m=√n and m=n²
rows.operation_detail: Compared minimum-norm test error across feature-to-sample ratios.

conditions.value: various values around and away from 1

rows.value: Minimum-norm solutions perform much better farther from the transition point; overfitting is much reduced at γ=0.9 or 1.1. At γ=1/2 or 2, minimum-norm test error is only a few times larger than the best value along the GD path. No appreciable overfitting is observed when m is O(√n) or O(n²).
rows.note: The paper gives qualitative comparisons; the figure does not supply stated numerical values for the curves.
rows.check: Overfitting of the min-norm solution is concentrated at γ=1 and drops sharply away from it, which matches a peak at the interpolation threshold. The source is Fig 3 (d=10 synthetic), with values only qualitative.

relation.reason: Its own experiments compare feature-count curves and training-time trajectories, and its analysis explains their dependence on small Gram-matrix eigenvalues.

tranche.reason: The study specifically qualifies the minimum-norm double-descent picture: small eigenvalues generate eventual overfitting but delay its development, largely suppressing the visible peak at practical training durations.

source_check.notes: Several row values and fixes are truncated in the pack; checks cover the visible assertions. The two V4 synthesis statements accurately describe this study's training-duration result; their other conditioning, privacy and resampling claims are not attributed to this study.

statements.correction: Figure 2: synthetic spherical inputs and ReLU features; d=10; m=n=500; gradient flow initialized at zero; small test error from t≈10^1 to t≈10^6; approaches minimum-norm error only after t>10^9; convergence takes nearly 10^10 time units. Figure 1: MNIST classes 0 and 1; n=500; d=784. Figures 4–5: slow deterioration across feature counts; no second temporal descent reported.
statements.problem: The qualitative slow deterioration is supported, but m=n=1024 and the stated 10^8 time horizon do not describe this study's Figure 2 experiment. This study contains no CIFAR10 experiment.
